```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

# Red Flags in Tendering {#sec-tenderflags}

The Health department of an imaginary State builds and repairs hospitals, health centres and staff quarters. Its divisions let about fifty works tenders a year. In each file the auditor finds a notice, a comparative statement, an approval and an agreement. Each file looks in order. Yet the department's contracts keep going to the same two firms. Many tenders received only one bid. Some notices gave bidders barely a week to respond. Was competition really open?

Questions like this are not about bidders quietly agreeing among themselves. They are about the **tendering process**. Who decided the procedure? Was the notice published? Was there enough time to bid? Did the scoring leave room for judgement? Did the price change after the award? A buyer who wishes to favour a chosen firm can restrict competition through any of these steps. Each step leaves a trace in the tender data, and each trace can be checked for every tender, however few bids it received.

This chapter is the first of three on tenders. It turns these traces into **red flags**, one rule for each step. It then combines them into a simple **corruption risk index** for each tender, department and firm. The next chapter, @sec-bidrig, looks for bidders acting together across many tenders. The one after it, @sec-bidshape, studies the shape of the bids within larger tenders and adds machine learning.

A red flag is not a finding. Many flagged tenders will have good reasons on file. The aim is to rank tenders by risk, so that the auditor reads the right files first.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Red flags in the tendering process {#sec-tenderflags-idea}

Mihály Fazekas and his colleagues have studied this problem with very large procurement datasets. In one well known study, Fazekas and Kocsis (2020) used about 2.8 million contracts from 28 European countries, awarded from 2009 to 2014.[^tf-fazekas] They define corruption in procurement as the unjustified restriction of access to contracts, to favour a chosen bidder. Such restriction cannot be seen directly. So they use two proxies.

- **Single bidding in competitive markets.** A tender that attracts only one bid, where many firms could have bid, is the plainest sign that access was restricted.
- **A composite score of red flags**, which they call the **corruption risk index** (CRI). It counts how many risky features a tender has.

Their red flags include the following.

| Step | Red flag | Why it matters |
|----------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Bidding | Only one bid | No competition at all |
| Notice | Call for tenders not published | Other firms could not know of it |
| Notice | A procedure other than open | Fewer firms are allowed to bid |
| Notice | A very short time to submit bids | Only a firm told in advance can prepare |
| Evaluation | A large weight on non-price criteria | Subjective marks can decide the winner |
| Award | An unusually short or long decision period | A rushed award, or a long delay for negotiation |
| Award | The procedure annulled and launched again | A second chance to get the "right" winner |
| Contract | Large modifications and increases in value | A low bid wins, and the price rises later |
| Buyer | The winner's share of the buyer's contracts | One firm takes much of the buyer's work |

: Red flags in the tendering process, following Fazekas and colleagues {#tbl-tenderflags-list}

Three points from their method matter for auditors. First, a red flag is kept only if it goes together with single bidding in the data. This checks that the flag really points to restricted competition. Second, the weight given to each flag is a judgement, or is estimated from the data. Third, the index ranks risk. It does not prove corruption. The World Bank has applied the approach to the procurement data of several countries, for example Bulgaria in 2023, and an open dataset of such indicators is published.[^tf-cri-data]

[^tf-fazekas]: Mihály Fazekas and Gábor Kocsis, "Uncovering High-Level Corruption: Cross-National Objective Corruption Risk Indicators Using Public Procurement Data", *British Journal of Political Science* (2020). [cambridge.org](https://cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-political-science/article/uncovering-highlevel-corruption-crossnational-objective-corruption-risk-indicators-using-public-procurement-data/8A1742693965AA92BE4D2BA53EADFDF0)

[^tf-cri-data]: The corruption risk indicators dataset, [datafinder.qog.gu.se/dataset/cri](https://datafinder.qog.gu.se/dataset/cri).

### The Indian setting

In India, most government tenders are now handled online. Central government tenders appear on the Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP). The States run their own e-procurement portals. Goods and many common services are bought through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM). The General Financial Rules of the Government of India, and the financial rules of the States, set out when an open tender is needed, when a limited or single tender may be used, and how long bidders must be given. They also require tenders to be published on the portal. The exact limits differ between governments and change over time.

So this chapter uses **example norms**, such as "open tenders stay open at least 21 days". The auditor must replace each one with the norm that governs the auditee. The OECD guidelines on bid rigging also list "too few bids where the market is large" as a warning sign. This is single bidding in a competitive market, seen from the other side.

## Our data, three years of tenders in five departments {#sec-tenderflags-data}

We have the works tenders of five departments of an imaginary State for 2022-23 to 2024-25. The departments are Public Works, Water Resources, Rural Works, Health and School Education. They work in five made-up districts, Amarpur, Bhimganj, Chandpur, Devnagar and Girinagar. Girinagar is a hilly, remote district with few contractors. The firms are made up too. `C01` to `C60` are general contractors, twelve based in each district. `C61` to `C65` build bridges. `C65` is the only bridge firm that works regularly in Girinagar.

The table `tenders` has one row per tender, with these columns.

- `tender_id`, `fy`, `department`, `district` and `work_type` (Road, Building, Bridge, Water works or Repairs).
- `procedure`. Open, Limited (invitation to selected firms), Single source, or Nomination.
- `published`, whether the notice appeared on the e-procurement portal.
- `publish_date` and `closing_date`, the date of the notice and the last date for bids.
- `estimate_lakh`, the estimated cost in ₹ lakh.
- `evaluation`. "L1 price" when the lowest price wins, or "Quality and cost" when marks for quality count too. `nonprice_weight` is the weight of the quality marks, in per cent.
- `n_bids`, the number of bids received, and `winner`, the firm awarded the contract.
- `award_date` and `award_lakh`, the date and value of the award.
- `retendered`, TRUE when an earlier call for the same work was cancelled and the work was tendered again. `first_call_l1` is the lowest bidder in that cancelled call.
- `final_lakh`, the value of the contract after all variations.

Genuine tenders behave as they do in real life. Fewer firms bid in Girinagar, for bridges, for limited tenders and when the time to bid is short. More bids bring lower prices. Some contracts grow for genuine reasons. Five cases have been planted.

1. From 2023-24, the **Health** department gives many tenders a very short time for bids, awards them within days, and often uses heavy quality marks. Most of these tenders receive one bid, and two firms, `C07` and `C19`, win them.
2. The **Rural Works** division in Bhimganj **splits road works** into groups of limited tenders, each just below the open-tender limit of ₹25 lakh.
3. One firm, `C12`, wins a **large share** of the water works of Water Resources.
4. One firm, `C23`, wins Public Works contracts **well below the estimate**, and their value is then **raised by large variations**.
5. School Education often **cancels a call and tenders again**. In the second call, `C31` wins, though another firm was lowest in the first.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the tender data"
set.seed(2526)

depts <- c("Public Works", "Water Resources", "Rural Works", "Health", "School Education")
districts <- c("Amarpur", "Bhimganj", "Chandpur", "Devnagar", "Girinagar")
work_mix <- list(
  "Public Works"     = c(Road = 0.45, Building = 0.30, Bridge = 0.10, Repairs = 0.15),
  "Water Resources"  = c("Water works" = 0.75, Bridge = 0.10, Repairs = 0.15),
  "Rural Works"      = c(Road = 0.70, Bridge = 0.10, Repairs = 0.20),
  "Health"           = c(Building = 0.55, Repairs = 0.30, "Water works" = 0.15),
  "School Education" = c(Building = 0.60, Repairs = 0.40)
)

# Firms. Twelve contractors based in each district, and five bridge specialists.
firms <- tibble(firm = sprintf("C%02d", 1:65),
                base = c(rep(districts, each = 12), rep("Bridges", 5)),
                pull = round(runif(65, 0.5, 2), 2))
firms$pull[firms$firm == "C65"] <- 12   # the one bridge firm working in hilly Girinagar
pick_firm <- function(district, work_type) {
  pool <- if (work_type == "Bridge") filter(firms, base == "Bridges") else filter(firms, base == district)
  w <- pool$pull
  if (work_type == "Bridge" && district != "Girinagar") w[pool$firm == "C65"] <- 0.5
  sample(pool$firm, 1, prob = w)
}

n <- 1000
t <- tibble(
  department   = sample(depts, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.26, 0.20, 0.24, 0.15, 0.15)),
  district     = sample(districts, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.23, 0.22, 0.22, 0.21, 0.12)),
  publish_date = as.Date("2022-04-01") + sample(0:1060, n, replace = TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(work_type = map_chr(department, \(d) sample(names(work_mix[[d]]), 1, prob = work_mix[[d]])),
         estimate_lakh = round(case_when(
           work_type == "Bridge"  ~ rlnorm(n(), log(150), 0.5),
           work_type == "Repairs" ~ rlnorm(n(), log(9), 0.6),
           .default               = rlnorm(n(), log(40), 0.7)), 2))

# Example norm. Works of Rs 25 lakh or more go to open tender. Smaller works may use limited tenders.
u <- runif(n)
t <- t |>
  mutate(procedure = case_when(
           work_type == "Repairs" & u < 0.05 ~ "Nomination",
           estimate_lakh < 25 & u < 0.50     ~ "Limited",
           estimate_lakh >= 25 & u > 0.97    ~ "Single source",
           .default = "Open"),
         published = case_when(procedure == "Open"    ~ runif(n()) > 0.01,
                               procedure == "Limited" ~ runif(n()) < 0.90,
                               .default = FALSE),
         short = runif(n()) < 0.06,
         days_open = case_when(
           procedure == "Open" & !short    ~ sample(21:35, n(), replace = TRUE),
           procedure == "Open"             ~ sample(12:20, n(), replace = TRUE),
           procedure == "Limited" & !short ~ sample(14:24, n(), replace = TRUE),
           procedure == "Limited"          ~ sample(7:13, n(), replace = TRUE),
           .default                        = sample(3:10, n(), replace = TRUE)),
         nonprice_weight = if_else(work_type == "Building" & runif(n()) < 0.12,
                                   sample(c(20, 30, 40), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.45, 0.45, 0.10)), 0),
         decision_days = round(rgamma(n(), 4, 4 / 30)) + 3 +
           if_else(runif(n()) < 0.04, sample(60:120, n(), replace = TRUE), 0L),
         plant = "none")

# Planted 1. From 2023-24 the Health department hurries many tenders through.
# Short windows, quick awards, one or two bids, and two favoured firms.
h <- which(t$department == "Health" & t$district != "Girinagar" & t$publish_date >= as.Date("2023-04-01") &
             t$procedure %in% c("Open", "Limited") & runif(n) < 0.65)
t$plant[h] <- "health"
t$days_open[h] <- sample(5:10, length(h), replace = TRUE)
t$decision_days[h] <- sample(2:6, length(h), replace = TRUE)
t$published[h] <- runif(length(h)) > 0.2
q <- h[runif(length(h)) < 0.4]
t$nonprice_weight[q] <- sample(c(50, 60), length(q), replace = TRUE)

# Bids. Fewer bids in hilly Girinagar, for bridges, for limited and unpublished tenders,
# when the window is short, and when much of the score is not price.
t <- t |>
  mutate(lam = 2.6 * if_else(district == "Girinagar", 0.45, 1) *
           case_when(work_type == "Bridge" ~ 0.5, work_type == "Road" ~ 1.2, .default = 1) *
           if_else(procedure == "Limited", 0.8, 1) * if_else(published, 1, 0.6) *
           if_else(days_open < 14, 0.45, 1) * if_else(nonprice_weight > 30, 0.6, 1),
         n_bids = if_else(procedure %in% c("Open", "Limited"), 1L + rpois(n(), lam), 1L),
         winner = map2_chr(district, work_type, pick_firm))
t$n_bids[h] <- sample(1:2, length(h), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.25))
t$winner[h] <- sample(c("C07", "C19"), length(h), replace = TRUE)

# Planted 3. C12 wins a large share of the water works of Water Resources
w <- which(t$department == "Water Resources" & t$work_type == "Water works" &
             t$district %in% c("Amarpur", "Chandpur", "Devnagar") & runif(n) < 0.55)
t$plant[w] <- "c12"
t$winner[w] <- "C12"

# Planted 5. School Education cancels calls and tenders again, and C31 then wins
r <- which(t$department == "School Education" & t$procedure == "Open" & t$plant == "none" & runif(n) < 0.17)
t$plant[r] <- "retender"
t$winner[r] <- "C31"

# Award price. More bids, lower prices.
t <- t |>
  mutate(award_lakh = round(estimate_lakh * (1.03 - 0.03 * pmin(n_bids - 1, 5) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.04)), 2),
         retendered = runif(n()) < 0.05 | plant == "retender",
         first_call_l1 = case_when(
           !retendered         ~ NA_character_,
           plant == "retender" ~ map2_chr(district, work_type, pick_firm),
           runif(n()) < 0.5    ~ winner,
           .default            = map2_chr(district, work_type, pick_firm)),
         u2 = runif(n()),
         variation = case_when(u2 < 0.60 ~ 0,
                               u2 < 0.97 ~ rnorm(n(), 0.06, 0.06),
                               .default  = runif(n(), 0.25, 0.45)))
t$award_lakh[h] <- round(t$estimate_lakh[h] * runif(length(h), 1.00, 1.08), 2)
t$award_lakh[w] <- round(t$award_lakh[w] * 1.04, 2)

# Planted 4. C23 wins Public Works contracts low, and the value is raised later
p <- which(t$department == "Public Works" & t$work_type %in% c("Road", "Building") &
             t$district %in% c("Amarpur", "Bhimganj") & t$procedure == "Open" & runif(n) < 0.22)
t$winner[p] <- "C23"
t$n_bids[p] <- pmax(t$n_bids[p], 3L)
t$award_lakh[p] <- round(t$estimate_lakh[p] * runif(length(p), 0.78, 0.86), 2)
t$variation[p] <- runif(length(p), 0.35, 0.65)

t <- t |> mutate(final_lakh = round(award_lakh * (1 + variation), 2))

# Planted 2. Rural Works in Bhimganj splits road works into limited tenders just below Rs 25 lakh
split_start <- as.Date("2023-06-01") + sort(sample(0:600, 9))
splits <- map(seq_along(split_start), \(g) {
  k <- sample(3:4, 1)
  tibble(department = "Rural Works", district = "Bhimganj", work_type = "Road",
         publish_date = split_start[g] + sample(0:2, k, replace = TRUE),
         estimate_lakh = round(runif(k, 21.5, 24.95), 2), procedure = "Limited",
         published = runif(k) < 0.5, days_open = sample(8:15, k, replace = TRUE),
         nonprice_weight = 0, decision_days = sample(10:30, k, replace = TRUE),
         n_bids = sample(1:3, k, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.35, 0.15)),
         winner = sample(c("C15", "C15", "C20", "C22"), k, replace = TRUE),
         retendered = FALSE, first_call_l1 = NA_character_) |>
    mutate(award_lakh = round(estimate_lakh * runif(k, 0.99, 1.04), 2),
           final_lakh = round(award_lakh * (1 + if_else(runif(k) < 0.6, 0, runif(k, 0, 0.08))), 2))
}) |>
  list_rbind()

tenders <- bind_rows(t, splits) |>
  mutate(closing_date = publish_date + days_open,
         award_date = closing_date + decision_days,
         evaluation = if_else(nonprice_weight > 0, "Quality and cost", "L1 price"),
         fy = if_else(month(publish_date) >= 4,
                      paste0(year(publish_date), "-", year(publish_date) %% 100 + 1),
                      paste0(year(publish_date) - 1, "-", year(publish_date) %% 100))) |>
  arrange(publish_date) |>
  mutate(tender_id = sprintf("TN-%04d", row_number())) |>
  select(tender_id, fy, department, district, work_type, procedure, published,
         publish_date, closing_date, estimate_lakh, evaluation, nonprice_weight,
         n_bids, winner, award_date, award_lakh, retendered, first_call_l1, final_lakh)

# Keep only the table that the auditor receives
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), "tenders"))
```

Let us look at the data.

```{r}
glimpse(tenders)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_tenders <- nrow(tenders)
n_winners <- n_distinct(tenders$winner)
crore <- function(lakh) round(lakh / 100, 1)
indian <- function(x, d = 1) format(round(x, d), big.mark = ",", nsmall = d)
```

There are `r format(n_tenders, big.mark = ",")` tenders, worth ₹`r crore(sum(tenders$award_lakh))` crore at award, won by `r n_winners` firms. Here is how they are spread across departments and years.

```{r}
tenders |>
  count(department, fy) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = fy, values_from = n)
```

Before we start, let us add three columns that several flags need. Subtracting one date from another gives a number of days.

```{r}
tenders <- tenders |>
  mutate(days_open     = as.numeric(closing_date - publish_date),
         decision_days = as.numeric(award_date - closing_date),
         variation_pct = round(100 * (final_lakh / award_lakh - 1), 1))
```

`days_open` is the time bidders had, from the notice to the closing date. `decision_days` is the time from the closing date to the award. `variation_pct` is how far the final value of the contract rose above the award, in per cent.

## Flags from the notice {#sec-tenderflags-notice}

The first flags come from the notice inviting tenders. They are known before a single bid arrives.

### The procedure

An open tender lets any qualified firm bid. A limited tender invites only selected firms. A single source or nomination contract goes to one firm without competition. The rules allow each of these in proper cases. Limited tenders are common for small works, and nomination may be justified in a real emergency. So a non-open procedure is a flag, not a fault. Let us see how often each department used each procedure.

```{r}
tenders |>
  count(department, procedure) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = procedure, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nonopen <- tenders |>
  summarise(share = mean(procedure != "Open"), .by = department) |>
  arrange(desc(share))
```

Rural Works used non-open procedures the most, in `r round(100 * nonopen$share[1])`% of its tenders. This may simply reflect many small road and repair works. We will look closer in @sec-tenderflags-split.

### Publication on the portal

A tender that was never published could not be seen by most firms. For open and limited tenders, publication on the portal is expected. For single source and nomination it is not, so we leave them out of this flag. This is our first use of a rule that applies only to some tenders.

```{r}
competitive <- c("Open", "Limited")

tenders |>
  filter(procedure %in% competitive) |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), not_published = sum(!published),
            share = round(mean(!published), 3), .by = department)
```

Most unpublished tenders are limited tenders, where the invitation goes to a few firms. That makes them easy to give to a chosen firm. The Health department is a little higher than the rest. The question to ask in each case is simple. Who was invited, and why only these firms?

### Time to bid

A short time to bid favours the firm that knew about the work in advance. In our example State, the department's own norm is at least 21 days for an open tender and at least 14 days for a limited tender. Let us first try the rule on three made-up tenders. `case_when()` lets us apply a different limit to each procedure.

```{r}
tibble(procedure = c("Open", "Limited", "Nomination"),
       days_open = c(18, 18, 4)) |>
  mutate(short = case_when(procedure == "Open"    ~ days_open < 21,
                           procedure == "Limited" ~ days_open < 14,
                           .default = NA))
```

The same 18 days is short for an open tender and enough for a limited one. For nomination the flag is `NA`, which means "does not apply". Now for all tenders.

```{r}
norm_open <- 21
norm_limited <- 14

tenders <- tenders |>
  mutate(short = case_when(procedure == "Open"    ~ days_open < norm_open,
                           procedure == "Limited" ~ days_open < norm_limited,
                           .default = NA))

tenders |>
  filter(procedure %in% competitive) |>
  summarise(share_short = round(mean(short), 2), .by = c(department, fy)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = fy, values_from = share_short)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sh <- tenders |>
  filter(procedure %in% competitive) |>
  summarise(s = mean(short), .by = c(department, fy))
h22 <- sh$s[sh$department == "Health" & sh$fy == "2022-23"]
h25 <- sh$s[sh$department == "Health" & sh$fy == "2024-25"]
others_top <- sh |> filter(department != "Health") |> slice_max(s, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
```

In 2022-23 the Health department gave a short window in `r round(100 * h22)`% of its tenders, much like the others. By 2024-25 the share was `r round(100 * h25)`%. The highest share in any other department was `r round(100 * others_top$s)`%, in `r others_top$department` in `r others_top$fy`. Part of that comes from the split works we meet in @sec-tenderflags-split. @fig-tenderflags-days shows the days given to bidders in open tenders.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tenderflags-days
#| fig-cap: "Days given to bidders in open tenders. The dashed line is the example norm of 21 days. Only Health has a large group of tenders far below it."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
tenders |>
  filter(procedure == "Open") |>
  ggplot(aes(days_open)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = norm_open, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~department, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Days from notice to closing date", y = "Tenders") +
  theme_bw()
```

Whether each tender was open long enough can also be checked against the portal itself, as in @sec-web-days, which scrapes the dates from the portal pages.

### Weight of quality marks

When the lowest price wins, the decision is objective. When marks for quality also count, the evaluation committee has room for judgement. A large weight on such marks can decide the winner. We flag tenders where the non-price weight is above 30 per cent. This cut-off is again an example.

```{r}
tenders |>
  filter(evaluation == "Quality and cost") |>
  count(department, nonprice_weight) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = nonprice_weight, values_from = n, values_fill = 0,
              names_prefix = "weight_")
```

Other departments used quality and cost evaluation now and then for buildings, mostly with weights of 20 or 30 per cent. Only Health used weights of 50 and 60 per cent. With such weights, a bidder quoting a higher price can still win comfortably on marks.

## Single bidding where competition was possible {#sec-tenderflags-single}

A single bid is the clearest sign that competition failed. But it is not always a sign of wrongdoing. In a remote district, or for a specialised work, there may be only one capable firm. Fazekas and colleagues therefore look at single bidding *in markets where competition is possible*. The auditor must do the same. Let us start with the share of single-bid tenders, among open and limited tenders, in each department.

```{r}
comp <- tenders |>
  filter(procedure %in% competitive)

comp |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), single = sum(n_bids == 1),
            share = round(mean(n_bids == 1), 2), .by = department)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sb <- comp |> summarise(s = mean(n_bids == 1), .by = department)
sb_health <- sb$s[sb$department == "Health"]
sb_other <- range(sb$s[sb$department != "Health"])
```

Health stands out, with `r round(100 * sb_health)`% single bids, against `r round(100 * sb_other[1])` to `r round(100 * sb_other[2])`% elsewhere. But perhaps Health tenders are of a kind that attracts few bidders anyway? Let us see which markets are thin. Here is the share of single bids by district and type of work.

```{r}
comp |>
  summarise(share_single = round(mean(n_bids == 1), 2), .by = c(district, work_type)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = work_type, values_from = share_single)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
gb <- comp |> filter(district == "Girinagar", work_type == "Bridge")
cb <- comp |> filter(work_type == "Bridge")
```

Bridges get single bids often in every district, because few firms build them. Girinagar has more single bids than the plains districts for most kinds of work. In Girinagar, `r sum(gb$n_bids == 1)` of its `r nrow(gb)` bridge tenders got one bid. These single bids are innocent. They reflect a thin market, not a restricted one.

### Comparing with similar tenders

A fair test compares each tender with similar tenders. We take "similar" to mean the same type of work in the same district, whatever the department. For each tender, the share of single bids among such tenders is the chance that a tender like it gets a single bid. Adding these chances over a department's tenders gives the number of single bids we would **expect**. We then compare it with the number we **observe**.

```{r}
single_check <- comp |>
  mutate(expected_chance = mean(n_bids == 1), .by = c(district, work_type)) |>
  summarise(tenders = n(),
            observed = sum(n_bids == 1),
            expected = round(sum(expected_chance), 1),
            .by = department) |>
  mutate(ratio = round(observed / expected, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(ratio))

single_check
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sc_h <- single_check |> filter(department == "Health")
```

The Health department received `r sc_h$observed` single bids where tenders of the same type in the same districts would lead us to expect about `r sc_h$expected`. That is `r sc_h$ratio` times the expected number. The other departments are at or below what their mix of works would suggest. Health's single bids cannot be explained by remote districts or specialised works.

::: callout-note
## Why single bidding matters for the price

Single bidding is not only a sign. It also costs money. In our data, the median award was `r round(100 * median(comp$award_lakh[comp$n_bids == 1] / comp$estimate_lakh[comp$n_bids == 1]))`% of the estimate when only one firm bid, and `r round(100 * median(comp$award_lakh[comp$n_bids >= 4] / comp$estimate_lakh[comp$n_bids >= 4]))`% when four or more firms bid. Competition lowers prices, so its absence raises them.
:::

## Splitting below the open-tender limit {#sec-tenderflags-split}

In our example State, the department's own norm says that a work estimated at ₹25 lakh or more must go to open tender. Smaller works may use limited tenders. A division that wishes to avoid an open tender can split one work into parts, each just below the limit. We met the same trick for payments in @sec-pipes.

The first sign is bunching. Let us count the limited tenders whose estimate lies between ₹20 lakh and the limit.

```{r}
limit_lakh <- 25

tenders |>
  filter(procedure == "Limited") |>
  summarise(limited = n(),
            near_limit = sum(estimate_lakh >= 20 & estimate_lakh < limit_lakh),
            .by = c(department, district)) |>
  arrange(desc(near_limit)) |>
  head(5)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
lim <- tenders |>
  filter(procedure == "Limited") |>
  summarise(limited = n(), near = sum(estimate_lakh >= 20 & estimate_lakh < limit_lakh),
            .by = c(department, district)) |>
  arrange(desc(near))
```

Rural Works in Bhimganj had `r lim$near[1]` of its `r lim$limited[1]` limited tenders between ₹20 lakh and ₹25 lakh. No other office had more than `r lim$near[2]`. @fig-tenderflags-split shows the bunching.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tenderflags-split
#| fig-cap: "Estimates of limited tenders. The dashed line is the open-tender limit of ₹25 lakh. Rural Works in Bhimganj bunches just below it."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
tenders |>
  filter(procedure == "Limited", estimate_lakh < 40) |>
  mutate(office = if_else(department == "Rural Works" & district == "Bhimganj",
                          "Rural Works, Bhimganj", "All other offices")) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate_lakh)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = limit_lakh, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~office, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Estimate (Rs lakh)", y = "Limited tenders") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Tenders issued together

Bunching shows a habit. Splitting shows itself more directly when several such tenders, for the same kind of work in the same district, are issued within a few days of each other. To find these groups, we sort the tenders by date within each office and type of work. A new group starts whenever more than 3 days pass since the previous tender. `cumsum()` numbers the groups, because it adds 1 every time a new group starts.

```{r}
batches <- tenders |>
  filter(procedure == "Limited", estimate_lakh < limit_lakh) |>
  arrange(department, district, work_type, publish_date) |>
  mutate(gap = as.numeric(publish_date - lag(publish_date)),
         batch = cumsum(is.na(gap) | gap > 3),
         .by = c(department, district, work_type)) |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), first_date = min(publish_date),
            total_lakh = sum(estimate_lakh), winners = paste(unique(winner), collapse = " "),
            .by = c(department, district, work_type, batch)) |>
  filter(tenders >= 3, total_lakh >= limit_lakh)

batches
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bt <- batches |> filter(department == "Rural Works", district == "Bhimganj")
```

`r nrow(batches)` groups of three or more limited tenders were issued within days of each other, together worth ₹25 lakh or more. All `r nrow(bt)` belong to Rural Works in Bhimganj. They hold `r sum(bt$tenders)` tenders worth ₹`r round(sum(bt$total_lakh), 1)` lakh at estimate. `C15` appears among the winners of most of them.

::: callout-warning
## Caution

Several small works issued together are not always one work split up. A division may genuinely repair five different village roads in the same week. The files decide. Do the works lie on the same road, one after another? Was there one administrative approval for the whole, later divided? Was the technical sanction split on the same day? The data can only point to the groups worth reading.
:::

## The winner's share of a buyer's contracts {#sec-tenderflags-share}

A buyer that favours one firm will give it a large share of its work. Fazekas and colleagues use the winner's share of the buyer's contracts as a red flag. Here the buyer is the department. Let us compute each firm's share of each department's total award value.

```{r}
win_share <- tenders |>
  summarise(wins = n(), value = sum(award_lakh), .by = c(department, winner)) |>
  mutate(share = round(value / sum(value), 3), .by = department) |>
  arrange(desc(share))

head(win_share, 8)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ws_c12 <- win_share |> filter(department == "Water Resources", winner == "C12")
ws_c19 <- win_share |> filter(department == "Health", winner == "C19")
ws_c07 <- win_share |> filter(department == "Health", winner == "C07")
ws_c31 <- win_share |> filter(department == "School Education", winner == "C31")
```

Four firms lead the list. `C19` and `C07` together won `r round(100 * (ws_c19$share + ws_c07$share))`% of the Health department's award value. `C12` won `r ws_c12$wins` contracts of Water Resources, `r round(100 * ws_c12$share)`% of its value. `C31` won `r round(100 * ws_c31$share)`% of School Education's value. Below them come the bridge firms. A bridge firm may win only a handful of contracts, but each is large. In a market with five bridge firms, a share of ten per cent is natural.

Two cautions follow. First, compare like with like. A bridge firm's share should be judged among bridge works, not among all works. Second, one very large contract can give a firm a high share on its own. So, for the flag, we work out the share within each department and year, and we flag a contract when its winner took more than 15 per cent of the department's value that year from at least three contracts.

```{r}
share_year <- tenders |>
  summarise(wins = n(), value = sum(award_lakh), .by = c(department, fy, winner)) |>
  mutate(share = value / sum(value), .by = c(department, fy)) |>
  mutate(big_share = share > 0.15 & wins >= 3) |>
  select(department, fy, winner, big_share)

share_year |>
  filter(big_share) |>
  count(department, winner)
```

This gives the flag for every contract of those firms in those years. The bridge firms still appear once or twice. That is fine. A flag only asks a question, and the answer for a bridge firm is usually easy.

The same idea can be taken further with networks. @sec-netaudit links firms through shared owners, addresses and bank accounts. A buyer's "top firms" may turn out to be one business.

## After the award {#sec-tenderflags-after}

Three more flags come after the bids are opened.

### The decision period

A very quick award, a day or two after the closing date, leaves no time for a proper evaluation. A very long one may hide negotiation or pressure. We flag awards made within 7 days or after more than 90 days of the closing date.

```{r}
tenders |>
  summarise(median_days = median(decision_days),
            within_7 = sum(decision_days < 7),
            over_90 = sum(decision_days > 90),
            .by = department)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
dd <- tenders |> summarise(q = sum(decision_days < 7), .by = department)
```

Long decisions occur in every department, a few each year. Quick ones are another matter. Health made `r dd$q[dd$department == "Health"]` awards within a week of closing. The other four departments together made `r sum(dd$q[dd$department != "Health"])`.

### Cancelled and tendered again

A call may be cancelled for good reasons, such as too few bids or prices far above the estimate. But cancelling a call in which the "wrong" firm was lowest, and tendering again until the "right" firm wins, is a known way to favour a firm. Let us see, for each department, how often the winner of the second call was a firm other than the lowest bidder of the first.

```{r}
tenders |>
  filter(retendered) |>
  summarise(retendered = n(),
            l1_changed = sum(winner != first_call_l1),
            .by = department)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rt <- tenders |> filter(retendered, department == "School Education")
rt_c31 <- rt |> filter(winner == "C31")
```

School Education tendered again `r nrow(rt)` times, far more than any other department. Let us see who won those second calls.

```{r}
tenders |>
  filter(retendered, department == "School Education") |>
  count(winner, l1_changed = winner != first_call_l1, sort = TRUE)
```

`C31` won `r nrow(rt_c31)` of the `r nrow(rt)` second calls. In every one of them, a different firm had been lowest in the first call. The first call was cancelled, the work was tendered again, and `C31` won. The auditor should read the reasons recorded for each cancellation.

### Contract variations

A contract may grow because the work grew, or because the design changed after the award. But a firm can also bid low to win, expecting the value to be raised later. We look at variations in detail in @sec-tenderflags-variation. For the index, we flag a contract whose final value is more than 25 per cent above the award.

## A simple corruption risk index {#sec-tenderflags-cri}

We now have nine flags. Let us put them all in one table, one row per tender and one column per flag. Each flag is TRUE, FALSE, or `NA` where it does not apply. Flags about competition apply only to open and limited tenders.

```{r}
flags <- tenders |>
  left_join(share_year, by = c("department", "fy", "winner")) |>
  mutate(
    single      = if_else(procedure %in% competitive, n_bids == 1, NA),
    non_open    = procedure != "Open",
    unpublished = if_else(procedure %in% competitive, !published, NA),
    heavy_marks = nonprice_weight > 30,
    odd_decision = decision_days < 7 | decision_days > 90,
    retender    = retendered & winner != coalesce(first_call_l1, winner),
    variation   = variation_pct > 25
  ) |>
  select(tender_id, department, district, winner, award_lakh, single, non_open,
         unpublished, short, heavy_marks, odd_decision, retender, variation, big_share)

flags
```

The flags `short` and `big_share` were already made in earlier sections, so we only select them. Notice the flag `retender`. A tender called again is flagged only when the firm lowest in the first call did not win the second. `coalesce()` replaces a missing `first_call_l1` with the winner, so tenders that were never cancelled get FALSE.

### The index for each tender

The simplest index is the **share of applicable flags that are raised**. A tender with 3 flags raised out of 8 that apply scores 0.375. To compute it, we turn the flag columns into rows with `pivot_longer()`, and take the mean of each tender's flags, ignoring those that do not apply.

```{r}
cri <- flags |>
  pivot_longer(single:big_share, names_to = "flag", values_to = "raised") |>
  summarise(flags_raised = sum(raised, na.rm = TRUE),
            flags_apply = sum(!is.na(raised)),
            cri = round(mean(raised, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            .by = c(tender_id, department, district, winner, award_lakh))

cri |>
  arrange(desc(cri)) |>
  head(8)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
cri_top <- cri |> arrange(desc(cri)) |> head(20)
```

All 20 of the riskiest tenders belong to Health. `r sum(cri_top$flags_raised == 6)` of them raise six flags at once. A single bid, a short window, a quick award, heavy quality marks and a winner with a large share often come together.

### The index for departments and firms

The same index can be averaged over a department or a firm. Let us also weight by value, so that the index reflects where the money went.

```{r}
cri |>
  summarise(tenders = n(),
            mean_cri = round(mean(cri), 3),
            value_weighted_cri = round(weighted.mean(cri, award_lakh), 3),
            .by = department) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_cri))
```

```{r}
firm_cri <- cri |>
  summarise(contracts = n(), value_lakh = sum(award_lakh), mean_cri = round(mean(cri), 3),
            .by = winner) |>
  filter(contracts >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_cri))

head(firm_cri, 8)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
dept_cri <- cri |> summarise(m = mean(cri), .by = department) |> arrange(desc(m))
fc_top <- head(firm_cri, 8)
c23_rank <- which(firm_cri$winner == "C23")
c23_flags <- cri |> filter(winner == "C23")
```

Health has the highest mean index, `r round(dept_cri$m[1], 3)`, against `r round(dept_cri$m[2], 3)` for `r dept_cri$department[2]`, the next. Among firms with at least five contracts, the top of the list is `r paste(fc_top$winner[1:5], collapse = ", ")`. These are the two Health firms, `C15` and `C20`, two of the three winners of the split works in Bhimganj, and `C31`. `C23` ranks only `r c23_rank`th of the `r nrow(firm_cri)` firms, with a mean index of `r firm_cri$mean_cri[c23_rank]`. `r sum(c23_flags$flags_raised == 1)` of its `r nrow(c23_flags)` contracts carry just one flag, a large variation. We return to it in @sec-tenderflags-variation.

### Checking the flags against single bidding

How do we know the flags measure anything? Fazekas and colleagues check that each red flag goes together with single bidding. If tenders with a short window get single bids far more often than other tenders, the flag points to restricted competition. Let us run the same check on our competitive tenders, one flag at a time.

```{r}
flags |>
  filter(!is.na(single)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(non_open, unpublished, short, heavy_marks, odd_decision,
                 retender, variation, big_share),
               names_to = "flag", values_to = "raised") |>
  summarise(single_if_raised = round(mean(single[raised]), 2),
            single_if_not = round(mean(single[!raised]), 2),
            tenders_raised = sum(raised),
            .by = flag) |>
  arrange(desc(single_if_raised))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
val <- flags |>
  filter(!is.na(single)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(non_open, unpublished, short, heavy_marks, odd_decision,
                 retender, variation, big_share),
               names_to = "flag", values_to = "raised") |>
  summarise(yes = mean(single[raised]), no = mean(single[!raised]), .by = flag)
v <- function(f, col) round(100 * val[[col]][val$flag == f])
```

The flags from the notice pass the check well. Tenders with a short window got a single bid `r v("short", "yes")`% of the time, against `r v("short", "no")`% for the rest. Unpublished tenders, heavy quality marks and odd decision periods show the same pattern. Two flags fail. Tenders with large variations had *fewer* single bids, `r v("variation", "yes")`% against `r v("variation", "no")`%. So did tenders called again.

This does not mean those flags are useless. It means they catch a different scheme. A firm that bids low and recovers through variations must beat real competitors to win, so its tenders have several bids. The check tells us what each flag measures. It also warns us against adding up flags that point in different directions without thinking.

::: callout-warning
## Caution, the index ranks risk

- **The weights are a judgement.** We gave every flag the same weight. Another team may weigh a single bid more than a long decision period. Decide the weights before looking at the results, write them down, and keep them fixed.
- **The cut-offs are a judgement too.** 21 days, 30 per cent, 25 per cent and 15 per cent are example norms. Use the auditee's own norms where they exist.
- **A high score is not proof.** A tender with four flags may have a perfectly good reason for each. The index tells the auditor which files to read first. It never replaces reading them.
- **A low score is not a clean chit.** A scheme that leaves no trace in these columns will not show up. The firm `C23` scores low, yet its contracts cost far more than they should.
:::

## Audit use case, a department where competition was restricted {#sec-tenderflags-health}

The index and the single-bid check both point to the Health department. Let us put together what we know, comparing its tenders from 2023-24 with those of 2022-23.

```{r}
health <- tenders |>
  filter(department == "Health", procedure %in% competitive) |>
  mutate(period = if_else(fy == "2022-23", "2022-23", "From 2023-24"))

health |>
  summarise(tenders = n(),
            single = round(mean(n_bids == 1), 2),
            short = round(mean(short), 2),
            quick_award = round(mean(decision_days < 7), 2),
            won_by_C07_C19 = round(mean(winner %in% c("C07", "C19")), 2),
            median_award_to_estimate = round(median(award_lakh / estimate_lakh), 3),
            .by = period)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
hp <- health |>
  summarise(n = n(), single = mean(n_bids == 1), short = mean(short),
            two = mean(winner %in% c("C07", "C19")),
            ratio = median(award_lakh / estimate_lakh), .by = period)
hp1 <- hp |> filter(period == "2022-23")
hp2 <- hp |> filter(period != "2022-23")
```

The change is sharp. In 2022-23, `r round(100 * hp1$single)`% of Health tenders got a single bid. From 2023-24 the share was `r round(100 * hp2$single)`%. Short windows rose from `r round(100 * hp1$short)`% to `r round(100 * hp2$short)`%. `C07` and `C19` won `r round(100 * hp1$two)`% of the tenders in 2022-23 and `r round(100 * hp2$two)`% afterwards. The median award moved from `r round(100 * hp1$ratio, 1)`% of the estimate to `r round(100 * hp2$ratio, 1)`%.

What did this cost? Let us take the Health tenders of 2023-24 onwards that `C07` or `C19` won with a single bid. We compare their award with what similar tenders cost in the other departments. Here similar means the same type of work, in the same district and year, with at least two bids.

```{r}
benchmark <- tenders |>
  filter(department != "Health", procedure %in% competitive, n_bids >= 2) |>
  summarise(usual_ratio = median(award_lakh / estimate_lakh), .by = c(district, work_type, fy))

health_cost <- health |>
  filter(period != "2022-23", winner %in% c("C07", "C19"), n_bids == 1) |>
  left_join(benchmark, by = c("district", "work_type", "fy")) |>
  mutate(usual_lakh = estimate_lakh * usual_ratio)

health_cost |>
  summarise(tenders = n(), award_lakh = sum(award_lakh),
            usual_lakh = round(sum(usual_lakh, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            no_benchmark = sum(is.na(usual_ratio)))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
hc <- health_cost |> filter(!is.na(usual_ratio))
hc_extra <- sum(hc$award_lakh) - sum(hc$usual_lakh)
```

On the `r nrow(hc)` tenders with a benchmark, the department paid ₹`r indian(sum(hc$award_lakh))` lakh. At the usual ratio of similar tenders, the same works would have cost about ₹`r indian(sum(hc$usual_lakh))` lakh. The difference is about ₹`r indian(hc_extra)` lakh. This is a rough indicator, not a loss. The benchmark is a median, and the works are similar, not identical. It is reported as the likely cost of the lost competition, with the method stated.

### What the auditor does next

1. **Read the files of the flagged tenders.** For each short window, look for the approval of the shorter period, by whom and for what reason. A real emergency should be recorded before the notice, not after.
2. **Check the portal.** Confirm the dates of publication and closing from the portal itself, as in @sec-web-days. A notice published late on the portal can make a long window in the register a short one in fact.
3. **Read the quality marks.** For each quality and cost evaluation, see who set the criteria and the weights, and whether the marks of each bidder are supported by documents.
4. **Ask who could have bid.** Use the list of firms that downloaded the tender documents, and the firms that bid for similar works in earlier years. Firms that looked and did not bid may be asked why.
5. **Look at the two firms.** Check their registration, owners and addresses, and any links between them, as in @sec-bidrig and @sec-netaudit.
6. **Report carefully.** State the facts. The share of single bids, the short windows, the quick awards, the two firms' share of the work, and the rough extra cost. Recommend that the department explain each restriction. Leave conclusions about intent to the competent authority.

## Audit use case, contracts won low and raised later {#sec-tenderflags-variation}

The index rated `C23` low. But one flag kept appearing on its contracts. Let us look at firms with at least five contracts, and compare how low they bid with how much their contracts grew.

```{r}
firm_var <- tenders |>
  summarise(contracts = n(),
            award_to_estimate = round(sum(award_lakh) / sum(estimate_lakh), 3),
            final_to_estimate = round(sum(final_lakh) / sum(estimate_lakh), 3),
            big_variations = sum(variation_pct > 25),
            .by = winner) |>
  filter(contracts >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(big_variations))

head(firm_var, 6)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
c23 <- tenders |> filter(winner == "C23")
fv23 <- firm_var |> filter(winner == "C23")
fv_next <- firm_var |> filter(winner != "C23")
```

`C23` is unlike every other firm. It won `r fv23$contracts` contracts, all in Public Works, at `r round(100 * fv23$award_to_estimate, 1)`% of the estimate on the whole. That is low enough to beat several bidders. But `r fv23$big_variations` of its contracts later grew by more than 25 per cent. In the end, its contracts cost `r round(100 * fv23$final_to_estimate, 1)`% of the estimate. No other firm had more than `r max(fv_next$big_variations)` large variations.

Let us list its contracts.

```{r}
c23 |>
  select(tender_id, fy, district, work_type, n_bids, estimate_lakh, award_lakh,
         final_lakh, variation_pct) |>
  arrange(desc(variation_pct))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
c23_raise <- sum(c23$final_lakh) - sum(c23$award_lakh)
c23_over_est <- sum(c23$final_lakh) - sum(c23$estimate_lakh)
```

Across its contracts, variations added ₹`r round(c23_raise, 1)` lakh to the award value. The final cost exceeded the estimates by ₹`r round(c23_over_est, 1)` lakh. The firm won because it was the lowest. Had the other bidders known that the quantities or items would change so much, the lowest bid might have come from someone else.

This pattern is sometimes called **bid low, recover later**. In item-rate works, a firm may quote very low rates on items it expects to be reduced, and high rates on items it expects to grow. If the department then increases those items, the firm gains. The pattern needs someone inside the department to make the variations happen, or at least to tell the firm in advance.

### What the auditor does next

1. **Read the variation orders.** For each large variation, see what changed, when, who proposed it, and who approved it. Was the change foreseeable when the estimate was made?
2. **Compare item rates.** For item-rate contracts, compare the rates quoted on the items that grew with the rates of other bidders and the Schedule of Rates. Rates far above the others, on exactly the items that later grew, are a strong sign. @sec-bidrig compares bills of quantities item by item.
3. **Re-rank the bidders.** Using the comparative statement, work out who would have been lowest if the final quantities had been tendered. If another firm comes out lowest, the cost of the variations to the department can be estimated.
4. **Check the delegation.** Confirm that each variation was approved by an authority with the power to approve it, and that cumulative variations did not cross a limit that needed higher sanction. Rule checks of this kind are set out in @sec-validate.
5. **Report carefully.** Present the pattern across all the firm's contracts, not one contract at a time, because the pattern is the finding.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip, getting the data

The flags in this chapter need data from several places. Ask for these, for every tender of the period, not only for the sample.

- **From the e-procurement portal.** The notice, the dates of publication and closing, the procedure, the evaluation criteria, the number of bids, the bid opening summary, and any corrigenda. Corrigenda that extend or shorten the window matter.
- **From the department.** The tender register, cancellation orders with reasons, approvals for limited, single source and nomination procedures, award letters and agreements.
- **From the accounts.** Variation orders, the final bill, and the total paid on each contract.

The register and the portal must then be matched, tender by tender. A tender in the register but not on the portal is itself a flag. Duplicates and mismatched tender numbers are common at this step, and the methods of @sec-dup help.
:::

## A suggested workflow

1. **Build one row per tender**, with the procedure, publication, dates, estimate, evaluation, bids, winner, award, cancellation and final value, from the portal and the department's records.
2. **Write down the norms** that govern the auditee, such as the minimum days for each procedure and the open-tender limit, before computing any flag.
3. **Compute the flags from the notice.** Non-open procedure, not published, short window and heavy quality marks.
4. **Check single bidding against similar tenders**, by type of work and district, so that thin markets are not mistaken for restricted ones.
5. **Look for splitting**, as bunching below the open-tender limit and as groups of small tenders issued together.
6. **Compute the winner's share** of each department's contracts, by year, and set aside specialised markets.
7. **Add the flags after the award.** Odd decision periods, calls cancelled when the "wrong" firm was lowest, and large variations.
8. **Combine the flags in an index**, with weights fixed in advance. Rank tenders, departments and firms.
9. **Check each flag against single bidding**, to see what it measures, and look separately at flags that catch other schemes.
10. **Read the files** of the highest-ranked tenders and firms, and report facts, not intentions.

::: callout-important
## Remember

- Red flags in the tendering process work for every tender, even one with a single bid. They need no bidding data beyond the count of bids.
- A single bid matters most where competition was possible. Compare with similar tenders before concluding anything.
- Every flag has innocent cases. Remote districts, specialised works and real emergencies are among them.
- The corruption risk index ranks risk. Its weights and cut-offs are judgements, and must be fixed before the results are seen.
- A flag that goes with single bidding points to restricted competition. A flag that does not may still catch another scheme, such as bidding low and recovering through variations.
- Report patterns and facts. Leave conclusions about corruption to the competent authority.
:::

## Where next

The next chapter, @sec-bidrig, turns from the buyer to the bidders, and looks for firms that act together across many tenders. @sec-bidshape then studies the shape of the bids within larger tenders, and shows how machine learning can combine many screens. Whether tenders were open long enough, checked against the portal itself, is in @sec-web-days. Rules such as delegation limits can be written as a rule book, as in @sec-validate. Matching the register with the portal often needs the methods of @sec-dup, and links between favoured firms can be traced as networks in @sec-netaudit.

## Try it yourself {#sec-tenderflags-exercises}

These exercises use the tables `tenders`, `comp`, `flags` and `cri` of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.

1.  **Short windows by year.** For open tenders only, find the median days given to bidders in each department and year. In which department and year was it lowest?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_days <- tenders |>
      filter(procedure == "Open") |>
      summarise(median_days = median(days_open), .by = c(department, fy)) |>
      arrange(median_days)
    head(ex_days, 4)
    ```
    The lowest median was `r ex_days$median_days[1]` days, in `r ex_days$department[1]` in `r ex_days$fy[1]`. A median below the norm means that more than half the open tenders of that department and year were short.
    :::

2.  **A thin market.** For bridge tenders in Girinagar, count the tenders, the single bids and the wins of each firm. Would you flag `C65` for its share?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_bridge <- comp |>
      filter(district == "Girinagar", work_type == "Bridge")
    ex_bridge |>
      summarise(tenders = n(), single = sum(n_bids == 1))
    ex_bridge |>
      count(winner, sort = TRUE)
    ```
    `C65` won `r sum(ex_bridge$winner == "C65")` of the `r nrow(ex_bridge)` bridge tenders in Girinagar, and `r sum(ex_bridge$n_bids == 1)` of these tenders got one bid. It is the only bridge firm based near the district, so a high share is expected. The auditor would note it, check the files of one or two tenders, and move on.
    :::

3.  **A wider gap for splitting.** Repeat the search for groups of limited tenders in @sec-tenderflags-split, but start a new group only when more than 10 days pass. How many groups are found now, and in which offices?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_batches <- tenders |>
      filter(procedure == "Limited", estimate_lakh < 25) |>
      arrange(department, district, work_type, publish_date) |>
      mutate(gap = as.numeric(publish_date - lag(publish_date)),
             batch = cumsum(is.na(gap) | gap > 10),
             .by = c(department, district, work_type)) |>
      summarise(tenders = n(), total_lakh = sum(estimate_lakh),
                .by = c(department, district, work_type, batch)) |>
      filter(tenders >= 3, total_lakh >= 25)
    ex_batches |>
      count(department, district)
    ```
    With a 10-day gap, `r nrow(ex_batches)` groups are found, holding `r sum(ex_batches$tenders)` tenders, against `r nrow(batches)` groups and `r sum(batches$tenders)` tenders before. Groups that were close in time have joined, and all are still in Rural Works in Bhimganj. The finding does not depend on the exact gap, which makes it stronger. The cut-off is still a judgement, and it is good practice to try more than one.
    :::

4.  **Different weights.** The audit team decides that a single bid should count twice as much as any other flag. Recompute the index for each department as a weighted mean, and see whether the order changes.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_weighted <- flags |>
      pivot_longer(single:big_share, names_to = "flag", values_to = "raised") |>
      filter(!is.na(raised)) |>
      mutate(weight = if_else(flag == "single", 2, 1)) |>
      summarise(cri = weighted.mean(raised, weight), .by = c(tender_id, department)) |>
      summarise(mean_cri = round(mean(cri), 3), .by = department) |>
      arrange(desc(mean_cri))
    ex_weighted
    ```
    Health stays first, with `r ex_weighted$mean_cri[1]`, followed by `r ex_weighted$department[2]`. The order of all five departments is the same as before, because Health is high on many flags at once. When two departments are close, a change of weights can swap them, which is why weights must be fixed in advance.
    :::

5.  **Riskiest tenders by district.** Using `cri`, find the number of tenders with an index of 0.3 or more in each department and district. Which office has the most?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_high <- cri |>
      filter(cri >= 0.3) |>
      count(department, district, sort = TRUE)
    head(ex_high, 5)
    ```
    `r ex_high$department[1]` in `r ex_high$district[1]` has the most, with `r ex_high$n[1]` tenders. Counting high-risk tenders by office is a simple way to choose which offices to visit.
    :::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `as.numeric(date2 - date1)` | base R | Days between two dates, such as days open and decision days |
| `case_when()` | dplyr | Applies a different norm to each procedure, and returns `NA` where a flag does not apply |
| `if_else()` | dplyr | Makes a flag that applies only to open and limited tenders |
| `mutate(.by = )`, `summarise(.by = )` | dplyr | Expected single bids from similar tenders, shares of a buyer's value, and summaries by department and year |
| `lag()`, `cumsum()` | dplyr, base R | Groups limited tenders issued within a few days of each other |
| `left_join()` | dplyr | Adds the winner's share and the benchmark ratio to each tender |
| `coalesce()` | dplyr | Fills a missing value, so that tenders never cancelled get FALSE |
| `pivot_longer()`, `pivot_wider()` | tidyr | Turns flag columns into rows for the index, and years into columns for display |
| `mean(na.rm = TRUE)`, `weighted.mean()` | base R, stats | The index as the share of applicable flags, and weighted by value or by flag |
| `geom_histogram()`, `geom_vline()`, `facet_wrap()` | ggplot2 | Days given to bidders and the estimates of limited tenders, with the norm marked |
